newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian fuel oil jittery in absence of China buyers.
newsitem.headline: Asian fuel oil jittery in absence of China buyers.

text.p: Singapore high sulphur fuel oil (HSFO) market was jittery Wednesday due to the prolonged absence of demand from China, but expectations of buying from a local trader is offering some underlying support, traders said on Wednesday.
"The Chinese have not come out to buy in a big way. They are playing it very cool," one trader said.
Traders said the eagerly awaited return of Chinese buying following the Lunar New Year holidays a week ago has yet to materialise and stocks are building up in Singapore.
Singapore weekly residue stocks for the week ended February 12 revealed a 645,000-barrel build in inventories to 10.06 million barrels, the Trade Development Board said.
The stocks include HSFO, low sulphur fuel oil, low sulhpur waxy residue and straight-run atmospheric residue stored in Singapore, excluding those kept in floating storage.
But these high stocks they said may be mopped up by a local trader who has yet to conclude term-contracts with Iran which runs out in February.
The company currently has contracts to lift around five 80,000-tonne cargoes per month from Iran, sources said.
Traders said if the two parties failed to agree on terms in time for the loading of March cargoes, the local trader might resort to buy from the local spot market which will drive prices up.
Fuel oil prices for 180-centistoke material last week firmed to around $104 per tonne free-on-board (fob) Singapore basis from a traded low of $93.00 per tonne on February 5.
Since the start of the week it has held steady at this level due to the uncertainties.
March fuel oil swaps traded on Tuesday at $103.00 per tonne down from Monday's $104.50 traded level. It was last quoted at $102.75/$104.00 per tonne, brokers said
Pressure on the market is also coming from the regular exports to the region despite the slow demand from China.
"We have a full March programme," one trader said.
On a monthly basis between five and seven 80,000-tonne cargoes are shipped to the region from the MidEast with arbitrage cargoes also seen sometimes from Venezuela or Mexico.
Together with the output from Singapore refiners, the majority of these cargoes are sold to the local bunker market and shipped to China.
Bunker demand has slowed down slightly as shipowners have held back purchases on expectations of further price cuts due to the lacklustre regional cargo demand.
Traders said China has already secured part of its March requirement from neighbouring South Korea and Japan and as a result is not aggressively seeking cargoes in the Singapore market.
"China talk is now centred on second half March not even first half March," one trader said.
Traders said bids from China are also at a low level of around $6-$7 per tonne premium to spot Singapore quotes on a cost-and-freight basis, compared to the $9 it paid in January.
--Singapore Newsroom (65-870-3093)
